new_rule.claim: AppleScript assigns stdout from a quiet HTTP curl command; not proof the response executes or communication succeeds.
new_rule.placement: HTTP response acquisition, method unspecified. Existing response-body leaf; no new taxonomy branch. No matching matcher found in the existing catalog.
new_rule.fixtures: Plain, parenthesized, escaped and -sS forms; unassigned fetch, file-only download, unrelated result assignment, different command and FTP near misses.
new_rule.consumer_audit: Inspected 11 ancestor-directory consumer sites: Crowd config traversal, multi-browser theft, free-TLD endpoints, Windows endpoint masquerade, cookie-path HTTP profiles/exfiltration, Windows raw-stage fiber execution, PE external-IP and Windows DLL composites. Windows/JVM-only consumers cannot accept this macOS rule. Other consumers still require their separate attack/path/host evidence; the new curl observation already implies the HTTP-client capability they select. No consumer or existing matcher was changed; all nine controls were checked for the new observation and scans show no new upstream findings.

analysis_limitations: Source flow graphs report limits and unavailable calls; source operands/control flow were manually traced.
Model bundle v18.18 uses feature version 18 while the engine expects 21; four destructive members remain below the calibrated alert grid (lvl -1) despite their hostile YAML findings.

No runtime success, user authorization history, AppleEvents/TCC grants, raw-device privileges, live server response or final downloaded stage was established. These are not prerequisites for the implemented malicious behavior.

Universal native/decoded-report variation changed neutral findings in initial cached runs. With the new YAML temporarily held outside rule discovery, fresh comparison reproduced the same differences, establishing they were not caused by the new matcher. Canonical uncached before/after comparisons retain every finding and add only the new notable rule in Installer and its archive ancestors.

The four small osinthell members each have one destructive result; all source statements and effects have existing supported findings. Shell execution, stream suppression, empty catches, raw disk writes and the separate bootrec repair command were investigated. No additional distinct hostile behaviors were found, so 3-5 hostile findings cannot be reached without duplicating or inventing attacks.
rule_classifier_disagreements: v.js, f.js, p.js and t.js are individually MALICIOUS with hostile rule detections but classifier-benign / no calibrated alert both before and after. No score inflation was used.

records.basis: individual bytes, source/control-flow and package context
records.marker_note: Installer: steals credentials; add curl output capture
evidence: Universal x86_64/arm64 Mach-O named Installer, packaged with an Archicad patch. No claim of family identity is needed for its malicious verdict.

ARM64 main at 0x100000690 obtains the decrypted command and calls system at 0x1000006b8. The helper copies 0x90dc bytes from __const+0xddc, passes seed 0x11667 and the following 37077 encrypted bytes to crypt. The loop XORs each byte with the low state byte, updating state as ((state*0x3785)&0xffffffff)%35999. Independent Python decoding matched both recovered 37076-byte command strings from cleave facts.
The command invokes osascript -e, joins source lines with return, and calls the final main handler. Long decimal handler names conceal names independently of native XOR encoding.

Main collects USER and hardware/software/display information, reads a home-directory cached password and validates it with dscl . authonly. If invalid it repeatedly requests a masked Installation password and validates the response. The captured password is cached and included in loot. An empty-password branch queries the Chrome generic-password Keychain item.

Copy helpers create destination directories, read the source and execute cat into the destination. Browser loops select Chromium Default/Profile stores and copy Cookies, Login Data, Web Data and selected wallet-extension Local Extension Settings/IndexedDB. Gecko code copies cookies.sqlite, formhistory.sqlite, key4.db and logins.json and locates MetaMask storage via prefs.js.

Copies desktop-wallet directories, login.keychain-db, a UUID-named Keychains folder, Notes databases/attachments and extension-filtered Desktop/Documents files. Finder is used for protected-file duplication. Notes property extraction is a fallback when the database copy is empty.

The actual stage directory is packed with ditto into /tmp/out.zip. curl --data-binary uploads that ZIP to an HTTP host configured in main. Stage and ZIP are removed after the upload call. The upload retry recursively omits its fourth parameter, so successful retries are not assumed.

Checks for Ledger Live, downloads a replacement ZIP, terminates the app, removes it using the captured password piped to sudo -S and extracts into /Applications. A separate helper captures a curl response, inserts that variable into shell ProgramArguments in a RunAtLoad/KeepAlive LaunchDaemon, writes/installs/bootstraps it using sudo, and falls back to an interpolated nohup command. UserName is the current user: root execution of the fetched command is not established.

New notable trait records the missing curl-output assignment. Existing findings already describe credential theft, file collection, upload, cleanup, unwanted app replacement, privilege abuse, persistence, obfuscation and launch primitives. No remote stage was downloaded or run.

records.basis: individual bytes, source/control-flow and package context
records.marker_note: parser-session writer: exports environment and evaluates HTTP reply
evidence: parser-session 1.1.9 writer.js, unrelated to a normal logging writer. On module initialization it spreads all process.env entries into data and adds subModuleVersion, platform, hostname, username and noninternal IPv4-interface MACs.

g replaces each pair of hex characters with String.fromCharCode(parseInt(pair,16)). The eight table slots resolve to require, axios, post, HTTPS endpoint, headers, X-header name, secret value and then.

The exported arrow ignores its arguments, requires the decoded Axios module, posts data as its second argument with the hidden header, and evals r.data in the then callback. Single-element array property keys coerce to the same decoded strings. The final catch discards rejection.

Concealed bulk environment export and remote-response execution are malicious functionality, independently of host-profile telemetry. Existing six hostile and six suspicious findings describe those sources, execution and concealment accurately.

As packaged ../package.json resolves to missing src/package.json; src/index.js also names a non-relative external .pnpm/httpreslog writer. These defects can block normal activation. No successful resolution, response payload or deployed execution is asserted.

records.basis: individual bytes, source/control-flow and package context
records.marker_note: osinthell v.js: silently deletes Windows System32 DLLs
evidence: osinthell 1.6.9 v.js exports a fixed zero-argument function. It invokes execSync with del /F /S /Q targeting C:\Windows\System32\*.dll through a shell, ignores stdio and catches errors without reporting them.

Forced recursive deletion of system DLLs serves no advertised OSINT or ordinary utility operation. The fixed sensitive target and silent action tip the verdict. Deletion success, administrator access and Windows runtime are not assumed.

All statements were traced. Existing hostile action and suspicious deletion-target/action profiles remain accurate. There is only one destructive objective; output suppression and exception handling are covered as notable capabilities, not additional invented attacks.

records.basis: individual bytes, source/control-flow and package context
records.marker_note: osinthell f.js: zeroes physical-disk boot sector
evidence: osinthell 1.6.9 f.js opens the raw PhysicalDrive0 device with r+, allocates exactly 512 zero bytes, writes that same buffer to that same descriptor at device offset zero and closes it.

A separate try block silently runs bootrec /fixmbr even if the raw write failed. The repair command cannot establish a benign purpose for zeroing the partition-table/boot-sector contents. It remains a notable repair command observation, separate from the hostile zero-write action.

All statements, operands and handle/buffer relationships were traced. Existing raw-disk open, first-sector zero-write, file-write and bootrec coverage suffice for the one destructive objective; there is no evidenced second attack to add. Runtime permission and repair availability are unknown.

records.basis: individual bytes, source/control-flow and package context
records.marker_note: osinthell p.js: truncates files across Windows drive roots
evidence: osinthell 1.6.9 p.js lists C:, D:, E: and F: roots, iterates returned entries, joins each to its root, tests the same path with statSync(...).isFile() and performs writeFileSync(path, empty string) with the destructive default write mode.

It truncates existing regular files at the roots; it does not recurse through directories, encrypt files, securely overwrite sectors or delete directory entries. Nested empty catches continue through drive/file errors.

The fixed unparameterized multi-drive action has no user-selected cleanup policy and implements destruction, not OSINT. Existing two hostile composites and suspicious bound-loop finding are retained. Every statement was reviewed; adding distinct hostile findings beyond that single objective would duplicate or invent behavior.

records.basis: individual bytes, source/control-flow and package context
records.marker_note: osinthell t.js: silently disables Windows boot recovery
evidence: osinthell 1.6.9 t.js exports a parameterless function executing bcdedit /set {default} bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures then bcdedit /set {default} recoveryenabled No, with shell execution, ignored stdio and an empty catch.

The two calls share one try: if the first throws, the second is skipped. The silent fixed recovery-sabotage pair and package-purpose mismatch tip the verdict. Each bcdedit setting alone has possible administrative uses, so the broader suspicious command observations remain accurate.

All statements and ordering were traced. This member implements one boot-recovery impairment objective, with no network, persistence, credential theft or automatic elevation. The hostile silent-action combination and three suspicious findings cover the supported attack. Successful BCD changes are unknown.
